nodes.title:
ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS
1. worker takes a job → hidden, not deleted
2. worker finishes → ack → deleted
3. no ack in 60 s → visible again
⚠ may run twice → make jobs idempotent

meta.title: Message Queues
meta.summary: Answer right away, do the slow work later — and never lose a job along the way.

goals.text: Why slow work doesn’t belong in a request

steps.title: Slow work inside the request
steps.body:
Creators upload videos, and each one must be transcoded into several sizes — about 30 seconds of heavy work. Right now the web server does it *inside* the upload request.

So the creator stares at a spinner for 30 s, many requests time out, and while servers grind through videos, every other page on the site slows down too.

callout.text: Anything slow, heavy or unreliable inside a request — video, email, reports, third-party calls — makes users wait for it.

steps.title: Put a queue in between
steps.body:
The web server now just stores the upload, puts a small **job** message on a [[message queue]], and replies at once: “processing — we’ll notify you”.

Separate [[worker]] machines pull jobs off the queue and transcode at their own pace. The web server is the **producer**; workers are **consumers**.

callout.text: Popular queues: RabbitMQ, Amazon SQS, Google Pub/Sub, and Kafka (a log that also works as a queue).

steps.title: A spike becomes a backlog
steps.body:
A big creator goes live and uploads jump tenfold. Without the queue, that spike would have flattened the web servers.

Now the web tier stays fast — it only enqueues — and jobs simply wait their turn. Workers keep a steady pace and catch up after the rush.

callout.text: A queue turns “too much work right now” into “a bit more waiting later”. This is called load levelling.

steps.title: Add workers to drain it
steps.body:
Need to catch up faster? Start more workers. They all pull from the same queue, and each job goes to exactly **one** of them — the [[competing consumers]] pattern.

Workers are stateless, so adding them is easy, and many teams scale them automatically on queue length.

callout.text: Producers and consumers now scale independently: add web servers for traffic, workers for processing.

steps.title: A worker dies mid-job
steps.body:
A worker crashes halfway through transcoding. If the queue deleted each job the moment it handed it out, that video is simply gone — the creator waits forever.

Machines crash, get restarted and are replaced all the time. The queue has to assume it.

callout.text: Handing out a job is not the same as finishing it.

steps.title: Acknowledge when done
steps.body:
Fix: a job is only *hidden* while a worker has it. When the worker finishes, it sends an [[acknowledgement]] and the job is deleted. No ack within a timeout? The job reappears and another worker picks it up.

The catch: a job can now run **twice** (say, a worker finishes but dies before acking). So jobs must be [[idempotent]] — safe to repeat.

callout.text: This is “at-least-once” delivery, the norm for queues. Exactly-once is very hard; idempotent consumers get you the same result.

steps.title: Poison messages and the dead-letter queue
steps.body:
One upload is a corrupt file. Every worker that tries it crashes or fails, the job is redelivered, and it fails again — forever, wasting workers and blocking others.

So queues count attempts. After, say, 3 failures the message is moved to a [[dead-letter queue]] (DLQ) for a human or a script to inspect.

callout.text: Alert on DLQ size. A growing dead-letter queue is often the first sign of a bug.

changes: ~ Failing jobs moved aside after 3 attempts

steps.title: Case: messages out of order
steps.body:
A different queue carries account events: `created`, `email changed`, `deleted`. With several workers pulling in parallel, a slow worker can finish “email changed” *after* another worker has already processed “deleted”.

Many queues give no ordering guarantee at all — and even ordered ones lose it once several consumers work in parallel.

callout.text: If correctness depends on order, you must design for it explicitly.

steps.title: Order per key with partitions
steps.body:
Systems like Kafka split a topic into [[partitions]]. Messages with the same key (say, the account id) always go to the same partition, and each partition is read by one worker, in order.

So events for one account stay in order, while different accounts are still processed in parallel across partitions.

callout.text: Order is guaranteed per key, not globally. Global order means one consumer — and no parallelism.

changes: ~ Events per account stay in order

steps.title: When the backlog never drains
steps.body:
Queues absorb spikes — but if jobs arrive faster than workers finish them *for hours*, the backlog grows forever. Jobs get older and older, and eventually storage runs out.

Watch queue **age**, not just length, and push back: autoscale workers, cap the queue, and tell producers to slow down (or reject new jobs with a clear “try later”).

callout.text: A queue buys time, not capacity. Long-term, throughput must match the arrival rate.

changes: + Queue capped · producers told to retry later

steps.title: Recap
steps.body:
• Move slow work out of the request: **enqueue** a job and answer immediately.
• Queues **absorb spikes**; add **workers** to drain the backlog.
• **Ack** after finishing; unacked jobs are retried — keep jobs **idempotent**.
• Park repeat failures in a **dead-letter queue**.
• Keep order **per key** with partitions; watch **queue age** and push back.

callout.text: Next up: **Pub/Sub & Events** — when one thing happening should trigger many others.
